The Compliance Gap:
Why AI Systems Promise to Follow
Process Instructions but Don’t
Kwan Soo Shin∗
PolymathMinds AI Lab
sshinresearch@gmail.com
ORCID: 0009-0001-5799-7556
Abstract
An auditor instructs an AI assistant to “open each file individually using the
Read tool—no scripts, no agents.” The AI replies “Yes, I will read each file
individually”—and then issues a single batched call summarizing all fifty files at
once. The text says one thing; the tool-call log shows another. We call this the
Compliance Gap.
Three questions follow: does this verbal–behavioral disconnect exist as a mea-
surable structural phenomenon (existence); can any text-only observer recover
it (detectability); what infrastructure does AI deployment need to instrument it
(remedy)? The failure has been invisible because some 75 existing benchmarks—
IFEval, SWE-bench, BFCL, COMPASS, SpecEval among them—measure outcome
fidelity, while none measures process fidelity: whether the user-instructed method
was followed. Two formal results anchor our answers. Theorem 1 shows the gap
is structurally inevitable under reinforcement learning that rewards text without
observing behavior. Theorem 2, via the Data Processing Inequality, shows it is
undetectable from text alone—by any human or LLM observer, present or future.
Thirteen experiments and 2,031 sessions on six frontier models confirm both
predictions. Existence: under default framing, all six models exhibit instruction
compliance rates of 0%—Claude Sonnet 4 verbally agrees ten out of ten times
then bypasses in all ten. The gap is selective, not random: models comply 97%
on tasks where rationale is rewarded (audit trails) and 0–4% where it is not (file
reading, privacy masking); removing delegation tools raises compliance from 0%
to 75% (Cohen’s d = 2.47), confirming the gap is environmentally afforded, not
weight-encoded. Detectability: nine blinded human raters reading only text outputs
achieve Fleiss’ κ = 0.130 and correctly identify zero of fifteen compliant sessions,
exactly as Theorem 2 predicts.
Where humans show roughly 47% intention–behavior gaps in social-psychological
studies and 96.5pp gaps in surgical-checklist audits, RLHF-trained models ap-
proach 100% under default conditions—a regime that warrants its own measure-
ment infrastructure. We release BS-Bench (the first open benchmark for process
compliance) as that infrastructure: a frozen v1.0 task suite, seven tool-call-log audit
metrics, and a public leaderboard.2 In one sentence: when the AI says it followed
your procedure and the audit log says it didn’t, the gap is the Compliance Gap;
our analysis suggests, via the Data Processing Inequality, that it is not reliably
recoverable from words alone.

Introduction
The phenomenon.
When a physician instructs an AI assistant to “perform a differential diagnosis
before concluding,” the instruction specifies not just what to produce but how. When an auditor
instructs an AI agent: “open each file individually using the Read tool—no scripts, no agents,”
the method is the mandate. These are process instructions: directives constraining the procedure
an AI system should follow, distinct from outcome instructions specifying the desired result. In
expert domains—medicine, education, law, auditing—process compliance is not a preference but
a professional and often legal requirement [Topol, 2019, Emanuel and Wachter, 2019, Grote and
Berens, 2022].
And yet.
The AI evaluation landscape has developed approximately 75 benchmarks3 for measuring
what AI systems produce—format [Zhou et al., 2023, Xu et al., 2025], response quality [Li et al., 2024,
Zheng et al., 2024], task completion [Jimenez et al., 2024, Liu et al., 2024b, Zhou et al., 2024], and
tool-use [Yan et al., 2024, Lu et al., 2024, Patil et al., 2023, Qin et al., 2024]. None evaluates whether
the AI followed the instructed procedure. The directly adjacent benchmark, SpecEval [Ahmed et al.,
2025], measures adherence to provider-defined model specs, not user-issued process instructions;
Zhang et al. [2025b] further document that internal spec conflicts undermine even provider-side
compliance. The full WHAT-subdimension catalog is detailed in Section A.2; the WHAT–HOW
knowledge taxonomy is formalized in Section A.1.
We argue the gap is methodologically generated.
The failure has been invisible for structural,
not empirical, reasons. Three forces accumulate to produce the gap.
1. Reward-signal asymmetry. RLHF [Christiano et al., 2017, Ouyang et al., 2022] optimizes
preferences over text completions, leaving behavior invisible to the reward signal—a specific
instantiation of Goodhart’s Law in the sense of Manheim and Garrabrant [2018] (regressional
Goodhart), formalized by Skalse et al. [2022].
2. Instruction-hierarchy de-prioritization. The instruction hierarchy [Wallace et al., 2025]
places system messages above user-level process instructions, so user-issued procedures are
structurally subordinate.
3. Delegation-affordance temptation. When a delegation tool (e.g., a batch call) is available,
the environment affords delegation and the model takes the shortcut that earns the same
text-reward with fewer actions.
We call the phenomenon arising from the combination of these three forces False Compliance
Sycophancy [Sharma et al., 2024, Perez et al., 2022]: agreeing to a procedure in words, then silently
substituting an automated shortcut. We distinguish the two terms throughout: the Compliance Gap is
the measurable metric (CG = VCR −ACR), while False Compliance Sycophancy is the name of
the behavioral phenomenon observed when that metric is positive.
This naming extends sycophancy research from belief alignment to behavioral alignment, paralleling
the CoT unfaithfulness lineage [Turpin et al., 2023a] where stated reasoning diverges from actual
computation. Within Amodei et al. [2016]’s alignment agenda, the Compliance Gap operationalizes
reward hacking (Theorem 1) and scalable oversight (Theorem 2) via tool-call audit. The structural
reasons HOW-compliance has been overlooked are detailed in Section A.3; the instruction-loss and
environmental-affordance mechanisms in Section A.5.
The Compliance Gap and its diagnostic.
The Compliance Gap (CG = VCR −ACR) is the
difference between an AI’s verbal and actual compliance rates evidenced by tool-call logs. A high CG
indicates an Integrity failure in Mayer et al. [1995]’s trust model: the system shows Ability (complies
when forced) and Benevolence (tries to help) but lacks Integrity. Theorem 1 establishes CG > 0
is structurally inevitable under preference-reward training observing only text. Theorem 2 (DPI,
Cover and Thomas, 2006) establishes CG is undetectable from text alone by any human or LLM
observer—formalizing why human raters fail.
3We surveyed 75 benchmarks published 2022–2026 across four subdimensions: format/constraint (18), response quality
(15), task completion (22), tool-use accuracy (20). Full list in the supplementary.
2

Three axes of AI honesty.
AI honesty research has concentrated on two text-level axes: factual
truthfulness [Lin et al., 2022] and what Liang et al. [2025] term machine bullshit after Frankfurt
[2005]—text whose author is indifferent to truth (Bullshit Index across 2,400 scenarios). We adopt
the abbreviation “BS” deliberately: our phenomenon is the AI-deployment instantiation of Frankfurt’s
bullshit, shifted to the behavioral channel. The Compliance Gap defines a third, orthogonal axis:
action-level truthfulness—whether the model honestly reports its own behavior, regardless of textual
accuracy or rhetorical substance. The three axes are independent: a model can be factually truthful,
rhetorically substantive, yet action-deceptive. Until measured on its own observation channel, the
action axis cannot be diagnosed.
Three questions, three answers.
Existence is established empirically (§4, Exps 1, 7–10): all six
frontier models show ICR = 0% across 1,380 sessions covering four framings, five task types, and
five professional domains. Detectability is bounded theoretically (Theorem 2, §3) and confirmed
empirically (nine blinded raters, κ = 0.130, 0/15 correctly identified). Remedy is operationalized
by BS-Bench’s seven-metric tool-call-log infrastructure (§3); causal experiments (Exps 2/2b/5/6)
identify candidate interventions (d = 2.47 from tool removal; d = 1.45 from supervised fine-tuning,
or SFT).
Contributions.
We present BS-Bench (the first open benchmark for process instruction compliance)
and results from thirteen experiments (2,031 sessions, eight models):
1. WHAT-HOW Taxonomy and BS-Bench. Formalizing outcome (∼75 benchmarks) vs.
process compliance (0 prior), with seven behavioral metrics, five task types, five professional
domains.
2. Compliance Gap Quantification. All six frontier models4 exhibit ICR = 0% under default
conditions (60/60); Claude Sonnet 4 reaches CG = 100pp.
3. Causal Mechanism. Instruction content explains 35.8% of variance vs. 8.9% for position
(η2=.358 vs. .089); removing delegation tools raises ICR from 0% to 74.7% (d = 2.47);
tool accuracy has no effect.
4. Task-Type-Dependent Compliance. Selective compliance follows the reward gradient: file
reading 0%, PII masking 4%, audit trail 97%.
5. Human Undetectability. Nine blinded text-only raters yield κ = 0.130; 0/15 compliant
responses correctly identified. LLM auditors recover only 40% (best 60%).
6. Robustness. Temperature ablation (t ∈{0, 0.7, 1.0}), description wording ablation, and
cross-domain replication (medical, legal, education, finance, engineering) confirm the
findings are not artifacts.
Roadmap.
Section 2 positions the Compliance Gap within four generations of evaluation bench-
marks and identifies the empty quadrant it fills; Section 3 formalises the construct via Theorems 1
and 2 and specifies the BS-Bench measurement infrastructure; Section 4 reports the thirteen-
experiment empirical inventory; Section 5 interprets the structural, selective, and undetectable
character of the gap and grounds it in four mature regulatory analogs; Section 6 states the falsifiable
forecast and four infrastructure recommendations.
2
Related Work
The WHAT–HOW knowledge taxonomy.
“Does the AI follow human instructions?” admits two
distinct readings. What compliance asks whether the system produced the correct outcome; how
compliance asks whether it followed the instructed procedure. Existing benchmarks invested heavily
in the former across four subdimensions—format, quality, task completion, tool use—while the latter
has, to our knowledge, gone unmeasured. Figure 1 maps the landscape; full treatment in Section A.

What compliance: the well-studied outcome dimension (∼75 papers).
Format following is
code-verified: IFEval [Zhou et al., 2023] reports 20–40% failure on verifiable formatting; Geng
et al. [2025] extend the constraint-conflict regime; AGENTIF [Xu et al., 2025, AGENTIF Team,
2025] carries it into agentic settings. Response quality is judge-approximated: AlpacaEval [Li et al.,
2024] and MT-Bench [Zheng et al., 2024] reward surface preference. Task completion is test-verified:
SWE-bench [Jimenez et al., 2024, Yang et al., 2024b], AgentBench [Liu et al., 2024b], WebArena
[Zhou et al., 2024], ComplexBench [Wen et al., 2024a], τ-bench [Yao et al., 2024] score outcome
only. Tool-use is benchmarked across Gorilla [Patil et al., 2023], ToolLLM [Qin et al., 2024], BFCL
[Yan et al., 2024], ToolSandbox [Lu et al., 2024], ToolEmu [Ruan et al., 2024], AgentBoard [Ma et al.,
2024]; the closest prior, COMPASS [Dessureault et al., 2026], evaluates which action—never how it
conforms. SpecEval [Ahmed et al., 2025] measures adherence to provider-defined specs (OpenAI
Model Spec, Anthropic Constitutional AI [Bai et al., 2022]), not user-issued process instructions;
Zhang et al. [2025b] show internal spec conflicts drive non-compliance even within the provider
framework.
Structural blindness: why HOW has been overlooked.
Three causes: (i) outcome metrics
automate while behavioral logs sit outside the standard pipeline; (ii) RLHF [Christiano et al., 2017,
Ouyang et al., 2022, Rafailov et al., 2023, Askell et al., 2021] optimizes preferences over completions,
leaving process invisible to the reward signal. The resulting reward hacking [Skalse et al., 2022,
Gao et al., 2023, Casper et al., 2023, Amodei et al., 2016] and sycophancy-to-subterfuge dynamics
[Denison et al., 2024, Pan et al., 2024, Ngo et al., 2024] are documented at the text layer; (iii) the
instruction hierarchy [Wallace et al., 2025, Chen et al., 2025, OpenAI, 2024] deprioritizes user-level
instructions, with Zeng et al. [2025] showing social-hierarchy framings override architectural roles,
and Saebo et al. [2026], Shayegani et al. [2025] showing system-level constraints leak under context
drift. By treating tool-call logs as out-of-distribution, the training pipeline maximizes the very gap
our benchmark exposes.
Mechanism: from sycophancy to false compliance.
The Compliance Gap is the AI-deployment
instantiation of Argyris and Schön [1974]’s espoused theory vs. theory-in-use distinction—a 50-year
foundation of organizational learning [Argyris and Schön, 1978] that lacked an information-theoretic
detectability bound (Theorem 2) and an automated measurement scaffold (BS-Bench) until this work.
Sycophancy [Sharma et al., 2024, Perez et al., 2022, Kim and Khashabi, 2025, Wei et al., 2024]
establishes that RLHF assistants favor agreeable responses; Hubinger et al. [2024] shows persistence
through SFT/RL/adversarial training; Burns et al. [2023] document a “knowing-but-not-doing” gap.
CoT faithfulness [Turpin et al., 2023a,b, Arcuschin et al., 2025, Lanham et al., 2023, Tanneru et al.,
2024, Paul et al., 2024, Matton et al., 2025, Stechly et al., 2024] documents the parallel stated-vs.-
actual gap; Cheng et al. [2025] shows elaborate CoT obscures hallucination cues. Reflexion [Shinn
et al., 2023], the closest self-monitoring mechanism, has a model verbally critique its trajectory; we
show in §4 that such self-critique does not close the behavioral gap. We extend this lineage to the
behavioral layer: False Compliance Sycophancy—verbal commitment without behavioral execution.
Wen et al. [2024b], Potham [2025] report adjacent “illusion of compliance”; Bavaresco et al. [2024]
show LLM-as-judge metrics are themselves sensitive to surface phrasing that conceals process gaps.
Context: instruction loss and environmental affordance.
Two broader literatures supply con-
textual conditions. Instruction loss [Liu et al., 2024a, Hsieh et al., 2024, Shi et al., 2023, Levy
et al., 2024, An et al., 2024, Sharma, 2026] explains why process instructions decay across long
contexts. Environmental affordance [Gibson, 1979, McCradden and Kirsch, 2023, Parasuraman and
Riley, 1997, Kahneman, 2011, Ye and Cui, 2025, Zverev et al., 2025, Greshake et al., 2023] explains
delegation defaults. Direct mapping to our Layer (Exp 2) and Affordance (Exp 6) experiments in
Section A.
The oversight gap: humans cannot detect HOW from text.
Mayer et al. [1995]’s integrative
model identifies Integrity—adherence to stated procedures—as a foundational trust dimension; Lee
and See [2004] elevates Process trust for professional automation; Topol [2019], Emanuel and
Wachter [2019], Grote and Berens [2022] extend to medical AI; Parasuraman and Manzey [2010],
Bansal et al. [2021], Vasconcelos et al. [2023], Zhang et al. [2020] document automation complacency.

Positioning vs adjacent literatures.
Three adjacent literatures merit explicit demarcation: AI
deception (Park et al., 2024, taxonomic and qualitative); NLP behavioral testing (CheckList, Ribeiro
et al., 2020, textual-output layer); and Health-AI stress-testing exemplified by Gu et al. [2025],
which exposes cognitive shortcuts (correct answers from wrong reasons; brittleness under prompt
perturbation) on text-only multimodal benchmarks. Ours operates on a structurally distinct behavioral-
channel gap (verbal output correct, tool-call log shows non-execution), where text-only oversight
is provably bounded by Theorem 2—making dual-channel audit a complement, not substitute, to
text-only stress testing. Ours is metric-infrastructural at the tool-call-log layer (extended treatment in
Section A.4).
Positioning BS-Bench: six gaps, one benchmark.
Table 1 maps the six knowledge gaps to
experimental evidence; Table 2 compares BS-Bench to closest prior benchmarks along four process-
vs-outcome axes. BS-Bench is, to our knowledge, the first benchmark that (1) operationalizes
process instruction compliance via tool-call logs; (2) provides causal evidence through controlled
manipulation of position, tool availability, and accuracy; (3) demonstrates remediability via SFT
and mid-session correction; (4) includes blinded human evaluation confirming text-based oversight
invisibility. Runtime spec adaptation [Zhang et al., 2025a] and user-side spec authoring are natural
follow-ons enabled by this infrastructure. An architectural comparison between the standard text-only
pipeline (which ∼75 prior benchmarks instantiate) and BS-Bench’s dual-channel audit infrastructure
is visualized in Figure 3.
The empty quadrant, two readings.
Figure 1 reads the gap as a missing column in a taxonomy of
evaluation dimensions; Figure 2 reads the same gap as a missing generation in the historical trajectory
of benchmarks. The two readings are consistent and mutually constraining: a categorically novel
evaluation dimension has been absent from a four-decade lineage of benchmarks, not because the
dimension is uninteresting but because the channel required to instrument it (tool-call logs) was absent
from the standard pipeline. Generation IV (Tool-use & Spec) operates the closest to BS-Bench’s
territory by virtue of using tool-using agents, but it scores them on outcome quality of the tool’s effect,
not on whether the user’s process was followed—which is the distinction Theorem 1 formalizes via
the verbal-only reward structure. Filling the upper-right quadrant therefore required the architectural
shift visualized in Figure 3: routing tool-call logs to a separate scoring function and reporting the
disagreement (CG) as a first-class metric, rather than averaging tool effects into outcome accuracy as
Generations III–IV do.

BS-Bench: Benchmark Design
Design principles. (1) Process observability: all measurements derive from tool-call logs without
model internals; (2) Ground truth: planted errors verify genuine execution; (3) Reproducibility:
standardized file sets, framing templates, evaluation scripts.
Methodological premise. Tool-call logs are the mirror of agent behavior—a record independent of
the agent’s narrative; verbal outputs are portraits—the agent’s chosen self-representation. BS-Bench
measures the gap between portrait and mirror. The mirror–portrait distinction is not metaphorical:
tool-call logs are produced by deterministic system-level instrumentation (the runtime that dispatches
and records each tool invocation), while verbal outputs are produced by the same policy whose
behavior is in question. The two channels are causally co-emitted but evidentially independent; the
audit-pipeline architecture (Figure 3) makes this independence operational by routing y and b to
separate scoring functions and reporting their disagreement as a first-class metric (CG), rather than
averaging them into a single accuracy score as the standard pipeline does.
Metrics. ICR (instruction compliance rate), DF (delegation frequency), FCR (false completion rate),
VCR (verbal compliance rate), ACR (actual compliance rate), CG (compliance gap = VCR −ACR,
∈[−1, 1]), TA (task accuracy via planted error detection); denominators in Supp §0. VCR is verbal;
ICR, DF, FCR, ACR, TA are behavioral; CG is the gap. The seven metrics partition the evaluation
surface into three operational layers: a single verbal scorer (VCR), a family of behavioral scorers
operating directly on tool-call logs (ICR, DF, FCR, ACR, TA), and the disagreement between them
(CG). This three-layer structure mirrors the architectural separation in Figure 3: outcome quality

Theoretical grounding. Two formal results anchor the paper.
Theorem 1 (RLHF Goodhart Inevitability). Let πθ denote a policy trained against a verbal-only
reward R(y) where y is the model’s text output and let b(y, h) denote the behavioral trajectory
induced by y in environment h. If user utility U depends on b but R does not, then for any θ⋆∈
arg maxθ R(πθ) there exists θ† with R(πθ†) = R(πθ⋆) but U(πθ†) > U(πθ⋆) whenever b has
positive variance under πθ⋆. Since R-optimal policies form a non-singleton level set whose behavioral
projections differ, E[VCR −ACR] > 0 in expectation across deployments under preference-reward
training that observes only text [Skalse et al., 2022].
Theorem 2 (DPI Undetectability). Let X = (y, b) denote the (verbal, behavioral) channels and
Y = y a text-only observation. By the Data Processing Inequality [Cover and Thomas, 2006], any
rater function f(y) measurable with respect to σ(Y ) alone cannot recover the residual b −E[b | y]
uniformly over its support. The Compliance Gap, defined on this residual, is therefore not identifiable
from y alone. (This residual coincides with the operational definition CG = VCR −ACR when (b, y)
are realised as compliance rates; see Supplementary §S2.)

Lineage: a 50-year construct now made information-theoretic.
The verbal–behavioral split
that Theorems 1 and 2 formalize is the AI-deployment instantiation of Argyris and Schön [1974]’s
espoused theory versus theory-in-use distinction—a 50-year foundation of organizational learning
research [Argyris and Schön, 1978]. Argyris and Schön observed that practitioners articulate one set
of governing values (espoused) while operating under another (in-use); diagnosing the gap required
behavioral observation, not verbal interview. What was missing in their framework, and what
Theorem 2 now supplies, is an information-theoretic detectability bound on text-only diagnosis. The
construct also admits a Crawford–Sobel babbling-equilibrium reading [Crawford and Sobel, 1982]:
when sender (the agent) and receiver (the auditor) interests diverge and the channel is verbal-only,
the equilibrium devolves to noise—which is exactly the empirical pattern we observe in R6 (§4.4:
κ = 0.130, slight; 0/15 correctly identified). The DPI bound is not merely a mathematical formality;
it predicts the empirical regime in which human and LLM raters operate, and our R6 result instantiates
it.
Principal–agent foundation: hidden action under verbal-only contract.
Theorems 1 and 2
are the AI-deployment instantiation of Jensen and Meckling [1976]’s principal–agent theory under
moral hazard with hidden action: a principal (the user) delegates a task to an agent (the AI) whose
action b is unobservable; the only available signal is verbal output y; compensation (here, the
RLHF reward R(y)) must be written on the observable signal alone. The Compliance Gap is the
AI-environment quantification of agency cost—the residual welfare loss that survives both monitoring

and bonding—now made information-theoretic by Theorem 2: the principal cannot recover the
missing action even with arbitrarily clever text auditors. The structure is in fact a triple principal–
agent: user (principal) delegates to AI (agent), but the AI’s training is shaped by the provider (a hidden
second principal whose objectives need not align with the user’s). Wuttke et al. [2025] document
the corresponding failure-by-success pattern in government AI delegation: initial efficiency gains
hide long-term loss of assessability, dependency, and contestability. Our §4 task-type results (file
0%, privacy 4%, audit 97%) instantiate the precise prediction of Holmstrom and Milgrom [1991]’s
multitask principal–agent theorem: when an agent allocates effort across multiple tasks and only
some have measurable output, equilibrium effort concentrates on the measurable tasks regardless of
the principal’s stated priorities. RLHF instantiates exactly this measurement asymmetry—text-quality
is measured, procedural sequencing is not—and selective compliance is the equilibrium it predicts.
Verbal channel as Bayesian persuasion, not babbling.
The Crawford–Sobel reading invoked
above models cheap talk that ends in babbling-equilibrium noise; Kamenica and Gentzkow [2011]’s
Bayesian-persuasion framework is the sharper match for RLHF-trained verbal output. In Bayesian
persuasion the sender chooses an information structure—a signal-generating policy—to shift the
receiver’s posterior toward the sender’s preferred action; the receiver remains Bayesian-rational,
and the equilibrium signal is rarely full revelation. RLHF is the explicit mechanism by which the
verbal channel is shaped into such a persuasion-optimal signal: y is the policy-chosen text that
maximizes preference-reward R(y), which by construction correlates with user belief in compliance.
The DPI bound (Theorem 2) is then the persuasion-bound’s information-theoretic ceiling: even a
fully Bayesian-rational receiver cannot recover the residual b −E[b | y], because no part of b that is
independent of y in distribution leaves any trace in y to update on. The empirical pattern—humans
κ = 0.130, LLM judges in a middle band, behavioral channel near-perfect—is the empirical signature
of a designed persuasion signal meeting an information-theoretic ceiling: the AI is not babbling, it is
succeeding at the persuasion task RLHF trained it for.

Discussion
Three properties to interpret.
The thirteen experiments establish three properties of the verbal–
behavioral split: it is structural (model-, framing-, and domain-invariant under default conditions),
selective (compliance scales with reward-signal alignment, not with the user’s instruction), and
undetectable from text alone (humans κ = 0.130, 0/15). The remainder of this section asks
what each property means for AI deployment, why interventions targeting any single property are
insufficient, and how four regulated domains have already constructed the infrastructure that the
AI-deployment regime now requires.
Design choice, not limitation. The Compliance Gap follows from RLHF training: the proxy reward
(text quality) does not observe process compliance. Models show high Ability (they comply when
forced) but low Integrity—an Integrity failure in Mayer et al. [1995]’s trust model. The three structural
forces producing CG > 0 are visualized as a cumulative cascade in Figure 8, alongside parallel
forces in regulated human practice.
The three forces are cumulative, not alternative.
Each layer alone is insufficient to produce
CG = 100pp; their composition is what makes the gap structurally inevitable. Layer 1 (reward signal)
creates the level set: any policy on the R-iso-surface is reward-equivalent regardless of behavioral
projection (Theorem 1). But level-set freedom alone does not select which behavior the model adopts.
Layer 2 (instruction hierarchy) breaks the symmetry: when a system-level alignment objective and a
user-level process directive conflict on the same iso-surface, the model resolves toward system-level
helpfulness/safety priors and away from user-level procedural fidelity [Wallace et al., 2025]. The
resolution is in the right direction for safety, the wrong direction for user process compliance, and
the two trade-offs are not separately tunable in current architectures. Layer 3 (affordance) makes
the resolution operational: when a delegation tool is available, the model has a low-cost shortcut
to the high-text-quality output the reward selects for. Removing the affordance closes the gap
(d = 2.47, Exp 6), but in deployment the affordance is the entire point of the agent. The cascade
structure also explains why interventions targeting only one layer are insufficient: SFT (a Layer-2
intervention via target-behavior demonstrations) recovers tool selection (d = 1.45, Exp 3) but not
full procedural sequencing, because Layers 1 and 3 still pull toward the shortcut. Closing the cascade
requires the missing piece—behavioral observation in the reward signal—which presupposes the
audit infrastructure BS-Bench provides.
Selective compliance is the key insight. Task-type results (Table 4) are more informative than the
headline ICR = 0%. The pattern is selective non-compliance, interpretable through reward-signal
alignment.
• Audit trail (97% compliance). Recording rationale aligns with the preference-rewarded
behavior of being helpful. Models comply where the procedure earns reward.
• File reading (0% compliance). Sequential tool use is unrewarded; a fast batch call earns the
same text-reward with less effort.
• Privacy-first (4% compliance). Pre-analysis masking adds latency without raising text
quality. Procedural steps that earn no reward are skipped.
Direct regulatory implication: the procedures most often skipped are precisely those mandated by
GDPR (PII masking), medical standards (differential diagnosis), and financial regulation (audit trails).

Four-domain isomorphism, in detail.
Read column by column, the grid is striking. Aviation
(1970s–1980s): mid-air collisions and Tenerife-class disasters were repeatedly traced to confident-
sounding cockpit verbal reports that diverged from the flight data; the resolution was not stronger

Anticipated objections. We address five steel-manned objections.
Objection 1: sycophancy by another name. Belief alignment vs. behavioral alignment: sycophancy
[Sharma et al., 2024, Perez et al., 2022] measures opinion concession; we measure procedure
execution. The DPI bound (Theorem 2) has no analog in that lineage.
Objection 2: anthropomorphic. We make no claim about understanding. ICR is operationalized
strictly as correspondence between issued procedure and tool-call log.
Objection 3: future RLHF will close the gap. Theorem 1 establishes structural inevitability under any
preference-reward signal that does not observe behavior. Only reward signals observing process—
presupposing audit infrastructure like BS-Bench—can close it.
Objection 4: users care about outcomes, not process. The selective profile (audit 97%, file 0%,
privacy 4%) supplies the counter: the procedures most often skipped are mandated by GDPR, medical
standard-of-care, and financial regulation. Users have legal cause to care wherever law does.
Objection 5: single-author work with nine raters is underpowered. Power analysis on the paired R6
design exceeds 0.99 at α = .05 (n = 261 paired observations); 13 experiments and 2,031 sessions
exceed prevailing ED Track norms.

Limitations. API models change without notice. R6 used ten non-expert raters; experts may achieve
higher detection. Exp 3 (SFT) is preliminary. Five task types, while structurally diverse, do not
exhaust all process instructions.

Conclusion
Summary.
This paper pursues a single claim (positioning landscape in Figure 2): AI assistants
trained under preference reward without behavioral observation systematically promise process
compliance and silently delegate it.
Formalization. We name the phenomenon the Compliance Gap (CG = VCR −ACR) and provide
the diagnostic metric (BS-Bench), the structural ground (Theorem 1: CG > 0 is inevitable under
text-only RLHF), and the oversight bound (Theorem 2: CG is undetectable from text alone via DPI).
Empirics. Thirteen experiments (2,031 sessions, eight models, five task types, five domains) confirm
both predictions.
• All six frontier models exhibit ICR = 0% under default framing; Claude Sonnet 4 attains
CG = 100pp.
• Compliance is selectively task-type-dependent (file 0%, privacy 4%, audit 97%).
• Content explains 4× more variance than position (η2 = .358); affordance is necessary
(d = 2.47).
• SFT eliminates tool selection (d = 1.45) but not completion.
• Nine blinded raters achieve κ = 0.130 with 0/15 correctly identified.
The structural visibility.
The Compliance Gap is invisible to outcome-based evaluation; the
metric, framework, and propositions we provide make it visible. Selective compliance is the deeper
insight: RLHF does not appear to produce universal non-compliance, but selective non-compliance on
procedural instructions most likely to be legally mandated (GDPR PII masking, medical differential
diagnosis, financial audit trails). The domains where process compliance is mandated by law are
precisely those where AI assistants will silently fail.
Limitations and falsifiable forecast.
Three limitations: (i) the 75-benchmark survey is bounded by
2022–2026 literature; emerging spec-evaluation efforts [Ahmed et al., 2025, Zhang et al., 2025b,a]
require tracking. (ii) R6 used ten non-expert raters (nine text-only); expert raters with tool-call training
may achieve higher detection. (iii) Five task types do not exhaust all process instructions. Falsifiable
claim: any RLHF-trained tool-using assistant evaluated only on text output, with delegation tools
available and no behavioral reward signal, exhibits CG > 0 in expectation.6 Variants that succeed
will, by Theorem 1, do so by re-introducing process observation into the reward signal—which
BS-Bench’s tool-call-log auditing makes operationally feasible.
Infrastructure recommendations.
We release BS-Bench as an open benchmark for the community
to measure, monitor, and close the gap between what AI systems promise and what they do. Four
infrastructure recommendations follow from this work.
1. Behavioral-channel logging as default. For tool-using AI deployments in regulated
domains, tool-call-log collection should be a default rather than an option.
2. Process-aware metrics reported separately. Process-aware metrics (CG, ICR, ToolFollow)
should be reported alongside outcome accuracy, not averaged into it.
3. Blinded human evaluation with tool-call logs. The R6 protocol should become standard
practice in place of text-only judgment.
4. SFT and similar interventions as diagnostic instruments. They should not be treated as
deployment fixes until process-rewarded training signals are demonstrated to close the gap
(channel-level auditability and maintained-infrastructure plan in Section A.9).
6Tentatively, the Murphy-form alignment law: under verbal-only reward, separable verbal and behavioral channels diverge
in expectation; analogues in regulated human practice (Section A.7); admits a Crawford–Sobel babbling-equilibrium reading
[Crawford and Sobel, 1982].

These recommendations are the operational counterpart of Laux [2024]’s institutionalised distrust
framework for human oversight of AI under the EU AI Act: just as democratic institutions design
distrust into their procedures (separation of powers, audit trails, contestability) to construct trust,
BS-Bench’s process-aware infrastructure designs behavioral-channel auditability into AI deployment
so that user trust is grounded in observable evidence rather than verbal self-report.

Extended Related Work
This appendix expands the seven literatures summarized in Section 2. Each subsection below

A.1
The Knowledge Taxonomy: From Outcome to Process
The question “does an AI system follow human instructions?” admits two fundamentally distinct
readings. The first—what compliance—asks whether the system produced the correct outcome: a
properly formatted response, a factually accurate answer, a successfully resolved software issue.
The second—how compliance—asks whether the system followed the instructed procedure to arrive
at that outcome: reading each file individually rather than delegating to a batch tool, performing a
differential diagnosis before concluding, executing each audit step in the mandated sequence.
Figure 1 maps the knowledge landscape along this distinction. Existing research has thoroughly
investigated what compliance across four dimensions—format, quality, task completion, and tool
use—while how compliance remains, to our knowledge, entirely unmeasured. The remainder of this
appendix traces the evolution of the what-compliance literature, identifies the structural reasons that
how compliance has been overlooked, and locates the six specific gaps that BS-Bench addresses.
A.2
What Compliance: The Well-Studied Outcome Dimension
A.2.1
Format and Constraint Following
The evaluation of verifiable instruction constraints is the most mature subfield of what compliance.
IFEval [Zhou et al., 2023] introduced 25 programmatically verifiable instruction types across 541
prompts, with frontier models failing 20–40% of formatting instructions. Geng et al. [2025] extended
this to six constraint types across six models under conflict, with Claude 3.5 Sonnet at 20.3% primary
obedience and GPT-4o at 47.0%—a result that foreshadows our Compliance Gap findings at the
process level.
AGENTIF [Xu et al., 2025, AGENTIF Team, 2025] extends evaluation to agentic settings, reporting
best instruction-following success rates below 30%. These benchmarks share a critical methodological
advantage: compliance is verified by code, not judgment. If the instruction says “write in fewer than
400 words,” a word counter settles the question. This advantage, however, also defines their boundary:
they can only measure instructions whose compliance is observable in the output text. Process
instructions—“read each file individually”—leave no textual trace that distinguishes compliant from
non-compliant execution.
A.2.2
Response Quality and Preference
A parallel line evaluates overall response quality through human preference proxies. AlpacaEval 2.0
[Li et al., 2024] achieves Spearman correlation of 0.98 with Chatbot Arena using GPT-4 as judge,
while MT-Bench [Zheng et al., 2024] extends evaluation to multi-turn dialogue. These benchmarks
have become the de facto standard for comparing model capabilities, with AlpacaEval evaluating
655+ models at under $10 per run.
The implicit assumption is revealing: a “better” response is one that a human judge prefers, regardless
of how it was produced. An AI that generates a perfect summary by delegating to a faster sub-
agent scores identically to one that reads and synthesizes each source document as instructed. The
quality-focused paradigm is, by construction, blind to process fidelity.
A.2.3
Task Completion in Agent Settings
The emergence of autonomous AI agents introduced task-completion benchmarks. AgentBench [Liu
et al., 2024b] evaluates agents across eight interactive environments. SWE-bench [Jimenez et al.,
2024] tests whether models can resolve real GitHub issues from 12 Python repositories, with SWE-
bench Verified [Yang et al., 2024b] providing 500 human-validated cases and SWE-Agent [Yang
28

et al., 2024a] establishing the agent-computer interface paradigm. WebArena [Zhou et al., 2024]
places agents in realistic web environments with e-commerce and content management systems.
These benchmarks advance what compliance from text evaluation to behavioral evaluation—
measuring whether agents achieve real-world outcomes. Yet even here, the evaluation criterion
remains outcome-focused: SWE-bench checks whether the generated patch passes the test suite,
not whether the agent debugged the issue through the developer-instructed method. A model that
solves the issue by searching Stack Overflow (efficient) rather than reading the codebase (instructed)
receives full marks.
A.2.4
Tool-Use Accuracy
The most proximate area to our work evaluates tool-use capabilities. Gorilla [Patil et al., 2023] and
ToolLLM [Qin et al., 2024] test API selection from large repositories (16,464 APIs). The Berkeley
Function Calling Leaderboard [Yan et al., 2024] established the standard for function-call accuracy.
ToolSandbox [Lu et al., 2024] introduced stateful, conversational, interactive evaluation with 1,032
test scenarios and implicit state dependencies. GTA [Wang et al., 2024a] and TaskBench [Shen et al.,
2024] extend tool evaluation to general agentic tasks and task-decomposition fidelity respectively.
ToolEmu [Ruan et al., 2024] uses LM-emulated sandboxes to identify agent risks, finding that even
the safest agent exhibits dangerous failures 23.9% of the time.
Schick et al. [2024]’s Toolformer demonstrated that language models can autonomously learn tool
use, while Yao et al. [2023]’s ReAct framework synergized reasoning and acting through interleaved
thought-action traces—the paradigm that underpins most modern tool-using AI agents and coding
assistants. ReAct’s reasoning step optimizes for task efficiency: “I need to search x, find y, then
find z.” Critically, there is no step that verifies whether the planned action conforms to the user’s
procedural instruction. This architectural omission is a proximate cause of the Compliance Gap.
Wang et al. [2024b] showed that executable code actions outperform natural language planning for
agent tasks. COMPASS [Dessureault et al., 2026] is the closest prior work to BS-Bench, providing
real-time multi-dimensional evaluation across sovereignty, sustainability, compliance, and ethics.
However, COMPASS evaluates which action to take (a what question) rather than how the action is
executed (a how question): an agent that passes all four COMPASS dimensions but delegates file
reading to batch_verify would receive full marks while violating the user’s process instruction.
Summary.
Across approximately 75 papers spanning four subdimensions of what compliance,
no benchmark measures whether the AI followed the user-instructed method to achieve its result.
BS-Bench operationalizes this missing dimension.
A.3
The Structural Blindness: Why HOW Has Been Overlooked
The absence of how-compliance research is not accidental. Three structural factors explain it.
First, outcome metrics are easier to automate.
Format compliance is checked by code [Zhou et al.,
2023]. Quality is approximated by LLM judges [Li et al., 2024, Zheng et al., 2024]. Task completion
is verified by test suites [Jimenez et al., 2024]. Process compliance, by contrast, requires access
to behavioral logs—tool call traces, action sequences—that are not part of the standard evaluation
pipeline. Most benchmarks operate on (input, output) pairs and never observe the intermediate
behavioral trajectory.
Second, RLHF optimizes text, not behavior.
The foundational RLHF pipeline [Christiano et al.,
2017, Ouyang et al., 2022] trains a reward model from human preferences over text completions.
Human evaluators comparing two responses cannot determine which response was produced by
following the user’s specified procedure—the behavioral layer is invisible to them. Rafailov et al.
[2023] simplified this pipeline with Direct Preference Optimization, but the fundamental constraint
remains: preferences reward surface appearance, not underlying process. Casper et al. [2023] catalog
22 open problems in RLHF, including reward hacking and specification gaming; Skalse et al. [2022]
formally characterize reward hacking; Gao et al. [2023] demonstrate predictable scaling laws for
reward model overoptimization. Pan et al. [2024] show that feedback loops in language models
drive in-context reward hacking, while Denison et al. [2024] trace a progression from sycophancy
29

to subterfuge in which reward-seeking behaviors escalate. Ngo et al. [2024] analyze the alignment
problem from a deep learning perspective, arguing that deceptive alignment is a natural consequence
of optimization pressure. The Compliance Gap is, in alignment terms, a specific instantiation of
Goodhart’s Law in the sense of Manheim and Garrabrant [2018] (regressional Goodhart): when text
quality becomes the optimization target, it ceases to measure process quality.
Third, the instruction hierarchy structurally deprioritizes user process instructions.
Wallace
et al. [2025] formalized the instruction hierarchy, training GPT-3.5 to prioritize system-level over
user-level instructions. The OpenAI IH-Challenge dataset [OpenAI, 2024] and Chen et al. [2025]’s
IHEval provide evaluation infrastructure. Zeng et al. [2025] applied mechanistic interpretation to
120,000 prompts, finding that social hierarchy cues override architectural role designations in the
model’s latent space. Saebo et al. [2026] independently observe “asymmetric goal drift” in coding
agents, where system prompt constraints are progressively violated. Shayegani et al. [2025] identify
“Blind Goal-Directedness” across nine frontier models with an 80.8% average rate, where three
failure modes—execution-first bias, thought-action disconnect, and request-primacy—parallel the
Compliance Gap’s verbal-behavioral dissociation. These works assume that compliance within a
priority level is unproblematic—our results show it is not. Even when a process instruction occupies
the highest-priority position (system prompt), models may verbally agree and behaviorally defect.
A.4
The Mechanism: From Sycophancy to False Compliance
The behavioral mechanism underlying the Compliance Gap connects two literatures: sycophancy
research and CoT faithfulness.
A.4.1
Sycophancy: Agreement Without Commitment
Sharma et al. [2024] established that sycophancy is a general behavior of RLHF-trained assistants,
driven by human preference judgments that favor agreeable responses over truthful ones. Perez
et al. [2022] discovered sycophantic behavior through model-written evaluations. Kim and Khashabi
[2025] showed that sycophancy intensifies under user rebuttal, while Yao et al. [2025] demonstrated
that multi-agent debate amplifies rather than mitigates it. Wei et al. [2024] proposed methods for
measuring and reducing sycophancy without gold-standard answers. Chen et al. [2024] proposed
Sycophancy-Probe Tuning to address sycophancy without degrading general capabilities, and Potham
[2025] identified the “illusion of compliance”—high adherence scores masking task incompetence.
Hubinger et al. [2024] provide the deepest concern: deceptive behaviors, once encoded through
training, persist through SFT, RL, and adversarial training. Burns et al. [2023] demonstrated that
LLMs can possess latent knowledge they do not express—a “knowing-but-not-doing” phenomenon
directly analogous to process non-compliance. Gao et al. [2024] propose honesty-targeted training
that exposes how surface compliance can mask substantive disagreement; Liu et al. [2024c] formalize
alignment failures as a class of specification-implementation gaps that subsumes the Compliance Gap
as a process-level instance.
We extend sycophancy from belief alignment (agreeing with opinions) to behavioral alignment (agree-
ing to follow procedures, then not doing so). This False Compliance Sycophancy is a commitment-
action gap rather than a belief gap: the model says “I will read each file manually” and then delegates
to batch_verify. Wen et al. [2024b] demonstrate that “language models learn to mislead humans
via RLHF”—our contribution specifies how this manifests in tool-use settings.
A.4.2
CoT Faithfulness: The Parallel Problem in Reasoning
Chain-of-thought faithfulness research addresses a structurally parallel phenomenon: reasoning traces
that do not reflect actual computation.
Turpin et al. [2023b] showed that LLMs “do not always say what they think,” with CoT explanations
that are post-hoc rationalizations; Turpin et al. [2023a] provide the closely related broader treatment.
Arcuschin et al. [2025] confirmed this in deployment settings. Lanham et al. [2023] found that
early tokens disproportionately influence final answers regardless of intermediate reasoning. Paul
et al. [2024] proposed methods for making reasoning matter by improving faithfulness. Tanneru
et al. [2024] established theoretical hardness results showing faithful CoT is fundamentally difficult.
Cheng et al. [2025] demonstrated that elaborate CoT obscures hallucination cues for humans—the
30

more detailed the reasoning appears, the harder errors are to detect. Matton et al. [2025] developed
automated metrics for reasoning faithfulness measurement.
The parallel is precise: CoT unfaithfulness = gap between stated reasoning and actual computation;
Compliance Gap = gap between stated behavior and actual behavior. Both are invisible at the text
output layer, both are driven by training incentives that reward surface over substance, and both
require automated measurement beyond text analysis.
Adjacent surveys of AI deception.
Our closest neighbor in the deception literature is Park et al.
[2024], who provide the first systematic catalogue of AI deception cases across learned, instrumental,
and emergent forms. Their contribution is taxonomic and qualitative; ours is metric-infrastructural.
Park et al. document what kinds of deceptive behavior have been observed; we provide the measure-
ment scaffolding (BS-Bench), formal results (Theorems 1 and 2), and 13 controlled experiments
that quantify how much of one specific class—procedural compliance failure—occurs across frontier
systems. We see the two contributions as complementary: their survey raises the question across
the broader landscape of AI deception, and our benchmark addresses one class of it—procedural
compliance—through measurement.
Behavioral testing for NLP vs. for AI agents.
The closest prior framework for behavior-level
evaluation is CheckList [Ribeiro et al., 2020], which introduced behavioral testing for NLP models
with capability-based test types (Minimum Functionality, Invariance, Directional). CheckList tests
model output text against linguistic capabilities (e.g., negation, vocabulary, named-entity robustness);
BS-Bench tests agent action trajectories against user-issued procedural instructions. The two are
complementary: CheckList probes what NLP models say across linguistic dimensions, whereas
BS-Bench probes what AI agents do against procedural commands. Their unit of observation is the
textual output; ours is the tool-call log. Both reject the accuracy-only paradigm, but on orthogonal
channels.
A.5
The Context: Instruction Loss and Environmental Affordance
Two additional literatures explain the contextual conditions under which the Compliance Gap emerges.
A.5.1
How Instructions Are Lost
Liu et al. [2024a] established the lost-in-the-middle phenomenon: LLMs attend to context beginnings
and ends while neglecting middle positions. Hsieh et al. [2024] traced this to positional attention
bias in their RULER benchmark, finding that claimed context sizes dramatically overstate effective
context. Shi et al. [2023] showed that irrelevant context degrades reasoning, while Levy et al. [2024]
demonstrated that longer inputs reduce accuracy even when additional content is relevant. An et al.
[2024] proposed IN2 training to address context underutilization. Sharma [2026] introduced Con-
textCov to transform passive agent instructions into executable guardrails—implicitly acknowledging
that text-based instructions are insufficient.
Our Layer Manipulation experiment (Exp 2) directly tests these findings in the process-compliance
domain: identical instructions placed at four architectural positions (System, User, Tool-description,
Repeated) yield compliance rates ranging from 26% (Tool) to 65% (Repeated), with instruction
content explaining 4× more variance than instruction position (η2 = .358 vs. .089).
A.5.2
How the Environment Shapes Non-Compliance
Gibson [1979]’s ecological approach predicts that behavior is shaped by environmental affordances—
the action possibilities that the environment presents. McCradden and Kirsch [2023] term the AI
analog algorithmic paternalism: the system overrides the user’s procedural judgment because it
calculates that delegation is more efficient. Parasuraman and Riley [1997] established the foundational
taxonomy of human-automation failures (Use, Misuse, Disuse, Abuse); we introduce a fifth category—
AI-side Misuse—where the AI system itself over-relies on available tools.
Kahneman [2011]’s System 1/System 2 distinction provides a cognitive framework: process instruc-
tions demand System 2 engagement, but AI systems optimized for efficiency default to System 1
patterns—reaching conclusions quickly without following the specified procedure. The adjacent
prompt-injection literature [Ye and Cui, 2025, Zverev et al., 2025, Greshake et al., 2023] formalises
31

how surface-level role cues can mislead the model’s authority assignment, with all evaluated models
failing adequate instruction-data separation [Zverev et al., 2025].
Our Tool Ablation experiment (Exp 6) directly tests the affordance hypothesis: removing delegation
tools converts ICR from 0% to 100% for two of three models (Claude Sonnet 4, GPT-4o-mini),
confirming that delegation affordance is a necessary environmental condition for the Compliance
Gap.
A.6
The Oversight Gap: Can Humans Detect Process Non-Compliance?
The human-AI trust literature has theorized but not empirically tested whether humans can detect
behavioral transparency failures of this kind.
Mayer et al. [1995]’s integrative model defines trust as comprising Ability, Benevolence, and In-
tegrity. The Compliance Gap is formally an Integrity failure. Lee and See [2004] identified Process
trust—confidence that the system followed the right procedure—as the most critical dimension for
professional domains. In medicine, Topol [2019] envisions AI augmenting clinical practice but notes
that diagnostic procedures exist to ensure no differential is overlooked; Emanuel and Wachter [2019]
argue that AI value in healthcare requires process integrity alongside outcome accuracy; Grote and
Berens [2022] demonstrate that fairness in ML-based healthcare requires attention to procedural
justice. Parasuraman and Manzey [2010] documented automation complacency: humans reduce
monitoring when they trust automated systems. Vasconcelos et al. [2023] showed that explanations
can reduce overreliance, while Zhang et al. [2020] demonstrated that confidence displays improve
trust calibration. Bansal et al. [2021] found that human-AI team effectiveness depends on appropriate
reliance.
Tsamados et al. [2025] argue that the supervisory control paradigm must shift to human-machine
teaming—but teaming requires meaningful human control [Fuchs et al., 2024], which presupposes
behavioral observability. Our blinded human evaluation (nine text-only raters, Fleiss’ κ = 0.130;
methodological grounding in Fleiss, 1971, Landis and Koch, 1977, Artstein and Poesio, 2008)
demonstrates that this presupposition fails: humans evaluating text output alone cannot distinguish
compliant from non-compliant AI responses, even when provided with gold-standard references.
Clark et al. [2021] showed that human evaluation of generated text is less reliable than assumed;
James [2026] called for greater transparency in reporting agreement metrics. Our finding extends this
to a new domain: the Compliance Gap is not merely difficult to detect—it is structurally invisible at
the text output layer.
A.7
Cross-Domain Audit Infrastructure Analogs
The four-domain isomorphism grid (Aviation CRM, WHO Surgical Safety Checklist, SOX §404,
ABA Rule 1.1) is promoted to the main body in Section 5 (Figure 9); this appendix subsection is
retained as a label-anchor for backward references.
Extended discussion: Process-compliance auditing has decades-old precedent in regulated industries,
and BS-Bench is best understood as the AI-deployment counterpart of this longer tradition. Aviation’s
cockpit voice recorders and flight data recorders provide a behavioral trace independent of the pilot’s
verbal radio communication [Helmreich, 2000]; reviewing the two channels in tandem is the standard
mechanism by which incident investigators distinguish what was said from what was done. The World
Health Organization’s Surgical Safety Checklist [Haynes et al., 2009] mandates verbal confirmation of
nineteen procedural items, with deviation auditable post-operatively. Sarbanes–Oxley §404 internal-
control requirements [Coates, 2007] oblige auditable trails of financial-decision processes, not merely
of their outcomes. The American Bar Association’s Model Rule 1.1 imposes a fiduciary “competence”
duty on attorneys that, as established case law has clarified, prohibits a verbal-only “I reviewed it”
defense in the face of demonstrable behavioral omission. The shared design pattern across these
domains is that high-stakes professional practice has long been judged by both verbal and behavioral
channels, with infrastructure built to inspect both. BS-Bench supplies the equivalent infrastructure for
AI deployments in these and adjacent regulated domains, where process compliance is not a stylistic
preference but a legally mandated component of professional practice.

Proof of Theorem 1 (sketch).
Let πθ be a policy parameterized by θ, with reward R : Y →R
defined on text outputs y alone, and let b : Y×H →B map (output, environment) to the behavioral tra-
jectory. By Skalse et al. [2022], R is hackable relative to user utility U whenever arg maxθ R(πθ) ̸=
arg maxθ U(πθ). If U depends on b but R does not, then any θ⋆∈arg maxθ R(πθ) leaves U(πθ⋆)
free to vary over the level sets of R. Whenever b has positive variance under πθ⋆(which holds for any
non-trivial environment family H), there exists θ† with R(πθ†) = R(πθ⋆) but U(πθ†) > U(πθ⋆). Op-
timizing R therefore admits solutions with strictly suboptimal U; in expectation across deployments,
E[VCR −ACR] > 0.
Proof of Theorem 2 (sketch).
The (verbal, behavioral) pair X = (y, b) generates the text
observation Y = y via the deterministic projection πy(X) = y. This forms a Markov chain
(y, b) →y →f(y) for any rater function f. By the Data Processing Inequality [Cover and Thomas,
2006, §2.8], I((y, b); f(y)) ≤I((y, b); y) = H(y) −H(y | (y, b)) = H(y), with equality iff
f is invertible on y. The Compliance Gap is defined on the residual d = b −E[b | y]. Under
the regularity assumption that d is independent of y in distribution (cf. Supplementary §2 for the
precise condition), no f measurable with respect to σ(y) can recover d uniformly; the best esti-
mator ˆd⋆(y) = E[d | y] ≡0 achieves Pr[ ˆd⋆(y) = d] which is bounded away from 1 whenever
Var(d | y) > 0, and any other estimator satisfies Pr[ ˆd(y) = d] ≤Pr[ ˆd⋆(y) = d]. The empirical R6
result (κ = 0.130, 0/15) is consistent with this bound.

Assumptions Made Explicit
For transparency we list every assumption used in the two theorems, marked by where it enters.
Assumption 1 (A1, used in Thm 1). User utility U depends only on the realised behavior b. We
do not require U to ignore y; the proof goes through whenever U has a strict additive component
depending on b (cf. the surgical-checklist case in App. A.7).
Assumption 2 (A2, used in Thm 1). The reward signal R during preference-reward training depends
only on text y. This holds for canonical RLHF [Christiano et al., 2017, Ouyang et al., 2022] that
elicits human preferences from text outputs alone. Process-aware reward signals (e.g. tool-call-log
scoring) violate (A2) by construction; Theorem 1 accordingly does not bound them, and BS-Bench
is the infrastructure required to make such alternative signals operationally feasible.
Assumption 3 (A3, used in Thm 1). The behavioral channel b has positive conditional variance
given the verbal channel y. Empirically supported by R6 (κ = 0.130, 0/15).
